# Lysosomal storage diseases

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric endocrinology and metabolism > Lysosomal storage diseases*

[Original Article Link](/library/dK0o2S)

---

## Summary

<u>Lysosomal</u> storage diseases are a group of inherited metabolic disorders caused by a deficiency of specific enzymes. This causes an accumulation of abnormal substances that are usually degraded within <u>lysosomes</u>, resulting in cell damage and <u>death</u>. These substances include specific lipids and glycoproteins such as <u>sphingolipids</u>, <u>glycosaminoglycans</u>, and <u>gangliosides</u>, among others. <u>Lysosomal</u> storage diseases have a progressive course and, depending on the exact disease and subtype, can also be fatal in early childhood.

## Sphingolipidoses

<u>Sphingolipidoses</u> are a group of <u>lysosomal</u> storage diseases caused by inherited deficiencies of <u>lysosomal</u> enzymes leading to alteration of sphingolipid <u>catabolism</u>. This will eventually lead to accumulation of pathologic <u>cellular inclusions</u> and cell damage, ultimately resulting in <u>cell death</u>. There are three main types of pathologic <u>cellular inclusions</u>:




* <u>Sphingomyelin</u>: derived from a <u>ceramide</u> with phosphorylcholine as a <u>hydrophilic</u> group

* Cerebrosides: derived from a <u>ceramide</u> with a single sugar residue (galactose or <u>glucose</u>)

* <u>Gangliosides</u>: derived from a <u>ceramide</u> with an oligosaccharide chain and one or more <u>sialic acids</u> linked to the chain





![Lysosomal storage disease](media/oj7oaio0gpfb648qqlwrezpw.jpg)

## Gaucher disease

* Etiology: <u>autosomal recessive</u> inherited disease [[1]](/library/mbYV8n)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Most common <u>lysosomal</u> lipid storage disease

* Increased <u>incidence</u> of type I in the <u>Ashkenazi Jewish population</u> [[2]](/library/bhXHcB)

* Pathophysiology: deficiency of β-glucocerebrosidase → accumulation of glucocerebroside (<u>sphingolipid</u> found in <u>cell membranes</u> that can accumulate in the <u>lysosome</u> of <u>macrophages</u>) in the <u>brain</u>, <u>liver</u>, <u>spleen</u>, and <u>bone marrow</u>

* Clinical features

* Vary according to the exact subtype of <u>Gaucher disease</u>

* Type I: non-neuronopathic <u>Gaucher disease</u>

* Type II: acute neuronopathic <u>Gaucher disease</u>

* Type III: chronic neuronopathic <u>Gaucher disease</u>

* All types

* <u>Hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* Bone: bone crises  , <u>osteoporosis</u>, <u>avascular necrosis</u> of the <u>femur</u>

* Blood abnormalities: <u>anemia</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>, <u>pancytopenia</u>

* Pulmonary manifestations

* Growth delays

* Type II

* Congenital <u>ichthyosis</u> (collodion baby), acute neurodegeneration

* <u>Death</u> within the first years of life [[3]](/library/XhX9cB)

* Type III

* Gradual onset of symptoms

* Neurodegeneration

* Diagnostics

* Reduced <u>glucocerebrosidase</u> activity in <u>leukocytes</u> or <u>fibroblasts</u>

* Accumulation of <u>glucocerebroside</u> in <u>leukocytes</u> or <u>fibroblasts</u>

* Gaucher cell: lipid-rich <u>macrophages</u> with an enlarged <u>cytoplasm</u> with <u>inclusions</u> that resemble crumpled tissue paper on microscopy

* Treatment: : enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant <u>glucocerebrosidase</u> or substrate reduction therapy with eliglustat





> [!NOTE]
> “The Girl HaS Painted A Bone Meticulously on a Crumpled Tissue Paper:” Glucocerebrosidase, HepatoSplenomegaly, Pancytopenia, Avascular <u>necrosis</u> of the <u>femur</u>, Bone crises, Macrophage <u>inclusions</u> that resemble crumpled tissue paper.

## Krabbe disease

* Etiology: <u>autosomal recessive</u> inherited disease [[4]](/library/lbYvFn)

* Pathophysiology: lack of or reduced activity of the <u>lysosomal</u> enzyme galactocerebrosidase (<u>GALC</u>; also called <u>galactosylceramidase</u>) → accumulation of galactocerebroside and psychosine (toxic <u>myelin</u> degradation products) and formation of globoid cells → <u>demyelination</u> and destruction of <u>oligodendrocytes</u> up to decerebration

* Clinical features

* Major mental and motor deficits

* <u>Developmental delay</u>

* <u>Peripheral neuropathy</u>

* Limb stiffness

* <u>Opisthotonic</u> posture

* Loss of <u>vision</u> (<u>atrophy</u> of the optical nerve)

* Diagnostics: globoid cell (a large multinucleated cell of mesodermal origin that is found clustered in the <u>brain</u> tissue   )

* Treatment

* Before symptom onset, <u>stem cell transplantation</u> may improve outcome.

* Only supportive treatment is possible after symptom onset.

## Tay-Sachs disease

* Etiology: <u>autosomal recessive</u> inherited disease [[5]](/library/NbY-Fn)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: : more common in the <u>Ashkenazi</u> Jewish population [[6]](/library/chXa1B)

* Pathophysiology: hexosaminidase A deficiency → <u>intracellular accumulation</u> of GM<sub>2</sub> <u>ganglioside</u> → progressive neurodegeneration

* Clinical features: Rapid reduction of physical and mental abilities begins around the age of 3–6 months [[5]](/library/NbY-Fn)

* <u>Developmental delay</u>

* <u>Macula</u> showing a “cherry-red” spot

* <u>Hypotonia</u>

* <u>Seizures</u>, <u>hyperreflexia</u>

* <u>Hyperacusis</u>

* Note: no <u>hepatomegaly</u> (unlike in <u>Niemann-Pick</u> disease)

* Affected individuals typically die around the age of 2–3 years [[5]](/library/NbY-Fn)

* Diagnostics: <u>lysosomes</u> with onion-<u>skin</u> appearance

* Treatment: supportive





> [!NOTE]
> “After they Hexed Tay's Sax, his playing became deficient.”

## Fabry disease

* Etiology: X-linked recessive inherited disease [[7]](/library/5bYi8n)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Typical onset is during childhood but may also appear in 60–80-year-old adults

* Mainly affects boys

* Pathophysiology: α-Galactosidase A deficiency → accumulation of ceramide trihexoside (also known as <u>globotriaosylceramide</u>; a <u>glycolipid</u> found in multiple body tissues) in the <u>endothelium</u> of vessels, in the <u>epithelium</u> of many organs, and in <u>smooth muscle cells</u> → disorder affecting many organ systems

* Clinical features

* Early symptoms manifest as a typical triad, consisting of

* Periodically occurring <u>dysesthesia</u>;  in the hands and feet caused by small fiber neuropathy , which manifests as burning <u>pain</u> (Fabry crises)

* <u>Anhidrosis</u> or <u>hypohidrosis</u>

* <u>Angiokeratomas</u>

* Other early symptoms include:

* Nonspecific gastrointestinal disturbances

* Corneal clouding

* <u>Cataract</u>

* Late symptoms

* <u>Cardiomyopathy</u>

* Cerebrovascular lesions (<u>TIA</u> and <u>stroke</u>)

* Fabry nephropathy, causing progressive <u>renal failure</u>

* Treatment: enzyme replacement therapy with α-galactosidase A





> [!NOTE]
> FABRYC: Foamy urine (Fabry nephropathy), α-galactosidase A deficiency/Angiokeratomas, Burning <u>pain</u> in hands and feet, Really sweaty/dry, YX <u>genotype</u> (male), Cardio-Cerebrovascular disease/Ceramide trihexoside accumulation.

## Metachromatic leukodystrophy

* Etiology: <u>autosomal recessive</u> inherited disease [[8]](/library/KbYUun)

* Pathophysiology: arylsulfatase A deficiency → cerebroside sulfate accumulation in neural and non-neural tissue → progressive <u>demyelination</u> of the central and <u>peripheral nervous system</u>

* Clinical features

* Infantile onset

* Motor regression and <u>developmental delay</u>

* Impaired <u>memory</u>

* <u>Ataxia</u>

* <u>Hypotonia</u> and <u>hyporeflexia</u>

* <u>Optic nerve</u> <u>atrophy</u> → loss of <u>vision</u>

* <u>Flaccid paralysis</u> followed by <u>spastic paralysis</u>

* Childhood and juvenile onset

* <u>Ataxia</u>

* Neurocognitive and behavioral changes (e.g., worsening school performance)

* <u>Peripheral neuropathy</u>

* Treatment: supportive

## Niemann-Pick disease

* Etiology: <u>autosomal recessive</u> inherited disease [[9]](/library/MbYM8n)[[10]](/library/LbYw8n)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: type A and B are more common in the <u>Ashkenazi</u> Jewish population [[11]](/library/dhXo1B)

* Pathophysiology

* Type A and B: genetic deficiency of sphingomyelinase → accumulation of <u>sphingomyelin</u>

* Type C: defective NPC <u>proteins</u> (mainly NPC1)

* Clinical features

* Progressive neurodegeneration (mainly type A and C)  [[12]](/library/9SXNbB)

* Cherry-red spot in the <u>macula</u>

* <u>Hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Light microscopy</u>: lipid-laden <u>macrophages</u> (<u>foam cells</u>) in the <u>bone marrow</u>, <u>spleen</u>, and <u>liver</u>

* <u>Electron microscopy</u>: Zebra bodies (abnormal configuration of myelinoid membranes into parallel palisading lamellae in the <u>lysosomal</u> <u>cytoplasm</u> )

* Treatment: mainly conservative





> [!NOTE]
> “No Man Pictures the Sphinx Proudly Holding Cherries:” <u>Niemann-Pick</u> disease (Sphingomyelinase deficiency, Progressive neurodegeneration, Hepatosplenomegaly, Cherry-red spots in the <u>macula</u>).

## Mucopolysaccharidoses

<u>Mucopolysaccharidoses</u> are a group of metabolic disorders that result in the impaired breakdown of <u>glycosaminoglycans</u> (previously known as <u>mucopolysaccharides</u>), due to mutations in <u>lysosomal</u> enzymes. At least nine different types of <u>mucopolysaccharidosis</u> have been identified. The two most common conditions are <u>Hurler syndrome</u> and <u>Hunter syndrome</u>. [[13]](/library/qKaChl)[[14]](/library/IKaY3l)




| Overview of the most common <u>mucopolysaccharidoses</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br>Hurler syndrome (<u>mucopolysaccharidosis type I</u>) | <br>Hunter syndrome (<u>mucopolysaccharidosis type II</u>)<br> |
| Inheritance | <br>* <u>Autosomal recessive</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>X-linked recessive</u><br><br> |
| Pathophysiology | <br>* Deficiency of α-L-iduronidase (enzyme responsible for the <u>hydrolysis</u> of <u>glycosaminoglycans</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Deficiency of iduronate-2-sulfatase<br><br> |
| <br>* Accumulation of <u>glycosaminoglycans</u>, i.e., <u>heparan sulfate</u> (HS) and <u>dermatan sulfate</u> (DS)<br><br> |  |  |
| Clinical features | <br>* Occur in both conditions (typically milder in <u>Hunter syndrome</u>):<br><br>* <u>Developmental delay</u><br><br>* Facial dysmorphism: <u>frontal bossing</u>, elongated <u>skull</u> , flattened nasal bridge, broad nasal tip, thickened <u>gingiva</u>, <u>anteverted</u> nostrils, constant nasal discharge, spaced and protruded eyes.<br><br>* <u>Airway obstruction</u><br><br>* <u>Hepatosplenomegaly</u><br><br> |  |
| <br><br>* Corneal clouding<br><br>* <u>Hypertrichosis</u><br><br>* <u>Failure to thrive</u><br><br>* Dysostosis multiplex<br><br>* <u>Inguinal hernia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Aggressive behavior<br><br>* Hyperactivity<br><br>* No corneal clouding<br><br>* Pearly <u>papules</u><br><br>* <u>Carpal tunnel syndrome</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Diagnostics | <br><br>* Increased urinary levels of <u>dermatan sulfate</u> (DS) and <u>heparan sulfate</u> (HS)<br><br>* Enzyme assay to confirm specific enzyme deficiency (definitive test)<br><br><br> |  |
| Treatment | <br><br>* Symptomatic and <u>palliative treatment</u><br><br>* Enzyme replacement therapy<br><br>* <u>Bone marrow transplantation</u><br><br><br> |  |





> [!NOTE]
> “Hunters with good eyesight will catch the aggressive chupacabra active in TeXas:” Hunter syndrome (no corneal clouding, aggressive behavior, carpal tunnel syndrome, hyperactivity, and X-linked recessive inheritance).

## I-cell disease

* Definition: an <u>autosomal recessive</u> disease caused by a defect in <u>N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase</u> activity

* Pathophysiology
* Defective <u>N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase</u> → impaired <u>phosphorylation</u> of <u>mannose</u> residues of glycoproteins in the <u>Golgi apparatus</u> that should be transported to <u>lysosomes</u> (glycoproteins do not have <u>mannose</u>-6-<u>phosphate</u>) → extracellular secretion of these glycoproteins instead of delivery to <u>lysosomes</u> → inability to degrade <u>lysosomal</u> content → accumulation of abnormal <u>lysosomal</u> substances in the serum

* Clinical features

* Coarse facial features

* Corneal clouding : progresses to blindness

* <u>Gingival hyperplasia</u>

* <u>Claw hand deformity</u>

* <u>Kyphoscoliosis</u>

* Abnormal bone growth and restricted <u>joint</u> movements

* <u>Failure to thrive</u> (<u>growth failure</u> by 2 years of age) [[16]](/library/VhXG1B)

* <u>Developmental delay</u>

* Diagnostics

* Prenatal: low levels of N-acetylglucosamine-1-<u>phosphodiesterase</u> enzyme activity in <u>amniotic fluid</u> or <u>chorionic villi</u>

* Postnatal

* Increased plasma levels of <u>lysosomal</u> enzymes

* <u>Inclusion bodies</u> in peripheral blood <u>lymphocytes</u> (I-cells)

* Note: negative urinary <u>glycosaminoglycans</u> (compared with <u>mucopolysaccharidoses</u>)

* Low levels of N-acetylglucosamine-1-<u>phosphodiesterase</u> activity in <u>white blood cells</u>

* Decreased concentration of <u>lysosomal</u> enzymes in cultured <u>fibroblasts</u>

* Treatment

* No cure available

* Only symptomatic treatment

* <u>Nutritional support</u>

* <u>Physical therapy</u> for musculoskeletal problems

* Complications

* <u>Pneumonia</u>

* <u>Otitis media</u>

* <u>Congestive heart failure</u>

* <u>Atlantoaxial instability</u>

* Prognosis: Affected individuals typically die from cardiopulmonary complications during childhood.
